cards.headline: S[KO-] is right: White takes the ko first and Black needs one threat more. The checker said DEAD because its narrow search area leaves out the corner.

diagrams.caption: The tree's line to the leaf, marked S[KO-], with White to play; the checker said DEAD. White can take the ko by capturing the Black stone at B16. The checker's narrow search area counts a as a wall and b and c only as fringe points.

White 4 takes the ko, and Black 5 retakes after a threat elsewhere. White 6, White's best try, is no local threat, which settles the first research's doubt about KO−2: Black 7 captures the stone at A16 and ends the ko. Black 11 at A19, a wall in the checker's narrow area, forces White 12 to connect, and Black 13 captures four stones: Black lives.
Without a ko threat Black dies: after White 4 every Black move loses. Here White 6 answers Black 5, and Black 7 can then retake without a threat, but too late: after White 10 Black is dead.

On an open board Black 5 threatens to run out at D15, yet it is no ko threat: after White 6 answers and Black 7 retakes, White 8 kills. After White 10 Black is dead, and every other Black move at 9 fails too.

text: The tree is right. White must take first, as any other White move lets Black live. Black then lives with a ko threat (Diagram 2) and dies without one (Diagram 3). Neither side has a local ko threat: not White 6 of Diagram 2, nor Black 5 of Diagram 4. So S[KO-].

As in the first research, the checker's mistake comes from its narrow search area, which leaves out the corner (Diagram 1): without the corner eye Black dies there even if it may ignore every ko ban, so the checker said DEAD. Its wider search area stayed undecided.
